rationale: Any authenticated user from any realm could force-disconnect another realm's MQTT session via GET disconnect/{sessionID}; no realm or role check. Contract has no operation entries.
Anonymous caller could retrieve usage report summary from /api/v1/usage-report/summary; handler lacked an authentication check. Path not seen in truncated contract.
Flawed Kubernetes NetworkPolicy for deployed instances; infrastructure network isolation, not an HTTP API operation.
Admin middleware let a request pass when the token lookup returned nil user without error, so admin endpoints were reachable with a non-empty invalid token. Contract declares ApiKeyAuth only.
User could duplicate a readable project under any parent project without write access to that parent; PUT duplicate path not visible in truncated contract.
User whose exec/create permission was revoked could keep sending terminal websocket messages in an open session; permissions not re-enforced. Terminal route not in swagger.
Users lacking Execute Code permission could configure TinkerpopClientService (script submission) via controller-service API; Restricted annotation missing. Contract has no operations.
Account could spend other accounts' balances through bonds messages by listing their address in its own DID verification method; signer not checked. Chain transactions, HTTP reachability uncertain.
Header-name constants let HTTP inbound headers override Camel route producer parameters; an injection/header-filter issue in an integration component, not a REST service access rule.
Anonymous or unauthorised user knowing an attachment UUID could download files of private repositories; no repository read check. Route absent from API contract.
Caller holding workflowrun:update for one component could PUT a run of another project/component by supplying own labels in the body; authz used body labels, not stored ones.
Generated pg_hba.conf trust entries for local Postgres connections; database host configuration, not an HTTP operation of the service.
Network policy parsing yields overly broad allow rule; data-plane traffic policy, not an HTTP API access decision.
Via mishandled error responses to proxied upgrade requests a client could reach backends using the API server credentials, escalating privilege. Specific operation not identified.
Egress policy derived from missing AWS security groups becomes broader; network policy semantics, not an HTTP API operation.
Anonymous client could PUT /api/echo/like/:id to increment like counts; route on public group. Provided diff touches OAuth redirect code, not this route.
